generated_by: a script run by hand over the committed text. The search is mechanical; the verdicts are authored; two judgements are made by hand and are marked where they are made — the `black` row, whose every early hit is the adjective and not a surname, and the list of which edit-distance-1 neighbours are names rather than ordinary words. Re-derivable: for each surname an apostrophe-tolerant word-boundary case-insensitive match over every line of data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt; the pre-1836 window is any line within eight lines of a line printing a year between 1820 and 1835; a zero result is re-tested against every word in the volume at edit distance 1 before it is called an absence.
_doc: T-0581's SECOND acceptance clause, discharged and shown. The Newberry genealogical index (T-0570) named forty-nine surnames standing BOTH on a lead in this project and on a Chicago or Cook County card that cites Moses and Kirkland. This file records that every one of them was looked up in the work itself — not a sample, not the promising ones. A surname with a verdict and no claim is a NEGATIVE RESULT and is the point of the file: it is what stops the next run paying for the same search twice.
window_note: THE PRE-1836 WINDOW IS A FILTER AND NOT A JUDGEMENT. It finds lines near a printed year, which is where a compiler dates its statements; it will miss a dateless sentence about the early town and it will catch a later paragraph that happens to mention 1835. Every claim in this domain was read in its own context, and the window only decided what to read.
zero_result_note: A ZERO RESULT IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY AN ABSENCE, because both sides of this search are OCR — the index cards T-0570 read, and this volume's own scan. The apostrophe cost one surname outright: a plain \b search reported `obrien` absent while the volume prints O'Brien, which is why the match is apostrophe-tolerant. Every remaining zero is re-tested at edit distance 1 against the volume's whole vocabulary, and the results split: where the neighbour is a surname the row is UNRESOLVED and names it, and where the neighbours are ordinary words the row is an absence.

counts.counts_note: The five verdict buckets do not partition the forty-nine on their own, because `black` is the one surname whose MECHANICAL verdict was READ and whose hand verdict is not: its early hits are the adjective. So 13 read + 8 present-and-early-not-claimed + 1 (black) + 21 present-but-late + 4 unresolved + 2 absent = 49. Every row keeps its mechanical verdict beside the authored one wherever the two differ.

volume_2: READ, T-0826, at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v2_lead_surnames.json. THIS FILE'S NEGATIVES WERE NEGATIVES ABOUT ONE BOOK OF TWO and said so; the companion file is the same forty-nine surnames looked up in volume 2 by the same script (tools/search_book_lead_surnames.py, whose --self-test re-derives every mechanical field of THIS file before it will run), and its `work_verdict_note` states what composing the two changed. In short: `gunn` is in the work after all, though still not in the early town; `nlan` is absent from both volumes and so from the work entirely; `gardiner`'s one-letter question was a fact about volume 1 alone, because volume 2 prints the card's own spelling. Nothing in this file was edited to say so — the rows below are volume 1's reading and stay as T-0581 wrote them.
